1
INTRODUCTION
For more than a half century, Alaska has tried to
stop the destruction caused by alcohol in its isolated,
rural communities. When alcohol was legalized following statehood, it ripped through remote villages .
Alcohol-related murders, violence, and accidents skyrocketed, with Alaska’s alcohol-related mortality rate
soaring to 418% above the national average. Local villages were largely defenseless. A typical village has no
police or emergency medical services and is inaccessible by road. When an alcohol-fueled event occurs, the
victims often have nowhere to turn.
To address this crisis , the Alaska legislature  authorized rural communities to prohibit the sale and
importation of alcohol. When villages adopt these restrictions, the State enforces them. And it does so in
predictable ways. In remote villages, alcohol often arrives by plane. So,  when the State charges and convicts a pilot for knowingly transporting alcohol into a
dry community, the law requires the forfeiture of the
airplane. By mandating forfeiture, the law prevents
the airplane from being used again to import alcohol
and deters others from doing the same.
Petitioner Kenneth Jouppi was convicted of knowingly transporting alcohol into the tiny and remote village of Beaver, where Jouppi knew alcohol was
banned. Jouppi’s crime was not flying in “a six-pack.”
Contra Pet-Br.2. Jouppi loaded two cases of beer and
four six-packs of 16-ounce beers on his plane destined
for a village of a mere 48 people with no roads in or
out and no emergency medical services. Because of his
criminal conviction, state law required forfeiture of
the plane.

2
As the Alaska Supreme Court correctly held, this
forfeiture did not violate the Excessive Fines Clause.
The Alaska legislature made a reasonable judgment
to mandate forfeiture to stop the scourge of alcoholinduced injuries and crimes in Alaska’s most isolated
villages. Jouppi fell within the class of defendants
principally targeted by the law . And the alcohol he
would have willingly flown  to Beaver had the potential to cause the exact harms feared by the legislature.
In his brief , Jouppi fights a strawman, insisting
that the Alaska Supreme Court considered his offense
“purely in the abstract.” Pet-Br.39-40. But the Alaska
Supreme Court held the forfeiture of Jouppi’s airplane
was constitutional as applied to Jouppi ’s actual circumstances. As the court observed, Jouppi attempted
to transport alcohol into a dry community. W hether
he knew about every case of beer he loaded onto his
plane or just the clearly visible six-pack, the constitutional analysis is the same . Faced with tragedy after
tragedy in Alaska’s remote villages, the Alaska legislature was well within reason to conclude that convicted defendants found beyond a reasonable doubt to
have knowingly violated Alaska law could have their
airplanes—the undisputed instrumentality o f that
crime—forfeited.
Alaska’s forfeiture regime is not unusual or extreme. At the Founding, Congress required the forfeiture of ships used to commit a host of crimes , including customs fraud, piracy, and the slave trade . Congress imposed similar punishments in Alaska when it
became a territory . Forfeiture of ships was the prescribed punishment for the illegal killing of fur -bearing animals  and the importation of alcohol . Those
laws, like Alaska ’s now, deterred hard- to-detect

3
crimes and incapacitated cri minals from using the
vessel to repeat the offense.
Nothing in our Constitution requires the Alaska
legislature to sit on its hands , allowing pilots who
knowingly transport alcohol into dry villages  to keep
their planes and do it again later. The judgment below
should be affirmed.
STATEMENT OF THE CASE
A. The Historical Use of Forfeiture in Alaska
With more land than Texas, California, and Montana combined, Alaska has never been easy to govern.
Since territorial days , Alaska has been  a “vast and
thinly populated region where it is difficult for law enforcement officers to detect and prevent smuggling
and poaching.” App.77a. Its geography has long presented an “open invitation to smugglers, as well as
those who would poach Alaska’s fish, game, birds, and
marine mammals.” App.77a. The “legislative response
to this problem —virtually from the time the United
States first acquired Alaska in 1867—has been to enact laws that call for the forfeiture of the marine vessels and (later) the aircraft used to commit smuggling
and poaching offenses.” App.77a.
Since Alaska’s first years as a U.S. territory, criminal punishments have included forfeiture of the instrumentalities used to commit those crimes. For example, Congress immediately prohibited the unauthorized hunting of fur-bearing animals in Alaska. Act
of July 27, 1868, ch. 273, § 6, 15 Stat. 240, 241. In addition to fines and imprisonment, the law mandated
that “all vessels … found engaged in violation of [the
law] shall be forfeited.” Id. Two years later, Congress
prohibited the unauthorized killing of certain seals on

4
islands near Alaska and again mandated that “all vessels … whose crews are found engaged in any violation
of [this law] shall be forfeited to the United States. ”
Act of July 1, 1870, ch. 189, § 5, 16 Stat. 180, 181.
The federal government ’s use of forfeiture in
Alaska continued into the next century and up to
statehood. See App.78a-80a. Various laws authorized
these types of forfeitures through both civil in rem and
criminal in personam proceedings. App.8 0a; see, e.g.,
Act of July 1, 1943, ch. 183, §5, 57 Stat. 301, 304 -05
(requiring forfeiture of “ boats, aircraft, wagons or
other vehicles” used to violate anti-poaching laws, either “upon conviction of the offender” or through an in
rem proceeding). Forfeiting the means by which
poaching and smuggling occurred was seen as essential to “ deter[ring] the violation of th[e]se laws .”
App.77a.
With respect to alcohol specifically, Congress took
immediate measures to keep alcohol and other contraband out of Alaska. Congress gave  the President the
power to “prohibit the importation … of fire-arms, ammunition, and distilled spirits into [the] territory.” Act
of July 27, 1868, § 6, 15 Stat. at 241. To enforce the
prohibition, Congress mandated that any vessel used
to violate the law “ shall be forfeited” when the value
of the contraband  on board exceeded $400. Id.; see,
e.g., The Louisa Simpson, 1 Alaska Fed. 50, 62 (D. Or.
1871) (forfeiting vessel whose captain traded “ liquor
to the Alaska Indians, in Kotzebue Sound, for the furs,
etc., found on the schooner, contrary to law, as he well
knew”). As in previous revenue laws, the $400 threshold served to ensure that the ship owner knew or had
reason to know about the contraband, because “[w]ithout the connivance of the master, goods to the amount

5
of $400 can hardly be smuggled from the ship. ” The
Harmony, 11 F. Cas. 556, 558 ( C.C.D. Mass. 1812)
(Story, J.). Through statehood, the United States continued to “emplo[y] both in rem forfeitures and in personam forfeitures of vessels and (later) airplanes to
punish and deter the smuggling of alcoholic beverages.” App.82a.
Today, Alaska continues to use forfeiture to deter
crime and prevent repeat offenders. But the form that
forfeiture proceedings take has changed over time.
Alaska has abolished “[c]ommon law civil in rem forfeiture actions … if used instead of a criminal proceeding.” Alaska Stat. §09.55.700. Although certain statutory civil in rem procedures remain on the books, this
type of forfeiture is almost never used in practice. See
H. Judiciary Comm. Meeting, 29th Leg., 2d Sess. (Apr.
4, 2016), perma.cc/L3JT-TMJ9. Instead, Alaska uses
criminal forfeiture, which, unlike civil forfeiture,  requires the State to prove the defendant’s guilt beyond
a reasonable doubt. See Culley v. Marshall , 601 U.S.
377, 395 (2024)  (Gorsuch, J., concurri ng). Criminal
forfeiture laws like Alaska’s enjoy “broad [public] support.” Okla. Governor Stitt Amicus Br. 9-10.
B. The Alcohol Crisis in Rural Alaska
Scattered throughout Alaska are about 225 isolated villages, each with an average population of just
300 people. Most villages are not connected to the road
system and are reachable  only by airplane, boat, or
snowmachine. Alaska Natives, the indigenous peoples
of Alaska, comprise a majority of the rural population.
See A Framework to Assess the Affordabi lity of Residential Water and Sewer Rates in Rural Alaska,
Alaska Dep ’t of Env’ t Conservation 13 (2020),
perma.cc/32DH-CPF8. Residents of these villages

6
regularly endure bone-chilling conditions unimaginable to most in the lower 48. See, e.g., Daily Situation
Report (Jan. 2, 2026) , perma.cc/7TKU-EBAV (warning residents in the Central Copper Valley to expect
“wind chills as low as 55 to 65 below zero ”). Most villages have no police department, no fire station, and
no emergency medical services. Village Public Safety
Officers, Dep ’t of Public Safety,  perma.cc/YY3Y-
6RDX.
For most of Alaska ’s territorial history, village
councils used their authority under the Indian Reorganization Act to prohibit alcohol in the rural villages.
See M. Berman, Alcohol Control by Referendum in
Northern Native Communities: The Alaska Local Option Law , 54 Arctic 77, 7 8 (Mar. 2001) . But w hen
Alaska joined the Union in 1959,  “village councils
found they could not enforce rules keeping alcohol out
of their communities because there were no state laws
against importation or possession. ” Id. Unlike tribes
in the lower 48, most Alaska Natives lack reservations
and thus depend on the State to enforce local laws. See
Yellen v. Confederated Tribes of Chehalis R srv., 594
U.S. 338, 342-43 (2021).
“As alcohol flowed more freely in rural areas during the next two decades, alcohol-related health problems grew rapidly among the Native population.” Berman, supra, 77. Individuals in rural communities
were especially vulnerable to alcohol abuse due to “the
great distances” from emergency medical services, “inclement weather,” and “lack of police services. ” Burnor v. State , 829 P.2d 837, 840- 41 (Alaska Ct. App.
1992). This growing crisis  “spawned a grassroots
movement calling for a change in policy.” Berman, supra, 79. “Village councils and elders, allied with

7
clergy, social service professionals, and law enforcement personnel serving rural Alaska, began to advocate [for] a comprehensive state response.” Id.
Between 1976 and 1980, the Alaska legislature received a se ries of state- sponsored studies that “ highlighted the massive problems that alcoholism and alcohol-related crime posed for the State of Alaska and,
particularly, rural Alaska. ” App.48a. Between 1959
and 1975, “Alaska’s rate of death due directly to alcoholism increased 153%” and Alaska’s alcoholism mortality rate was “418% higher than the national average.” Harrison v. State, 687 P.2d 332, 335 (Alaska Ct.
App. 1984). Studies found a “ significant relationship
between the use of alcohol and criminal behavior,” especially in rural areas of the State, where “77.9% of
violent crimes and 55.6% of property crimes were committed under the influence of alcohol.” Id. Over 30% of
the State’s criminal-justice budget was devoted to addressing alcohol- related crimes. Abraham v. State ,
585 P.2d 526, 532 n.19 (Alaska 1978).
Faced with these devastating findings, the Alaska
legislature in 1980 adopted a “ local option ” law authorizing villages to prohibit alcohol in their communities. Under the new law, villages could vote to prohibit the “sale and importation of alcoholic beverages”
in their community. Alaska Stat. §04.11.496(a) (1980).
If the referendum passed, then the s tate law prohibited a ny person from “ knowingly send[ing],
transport[ing], or bring[ing] alcoholic beverages into
the … village.” Id. §04.11.496(b). To “give teeth” to the
will of the electorate, App.86a, the new law gave sentencing courts the authority to order the forfeiture of
any “aircraft, vehicles, or vessels used to transport, or
facilitate the transportation of … alcoholic beverages

8
imported into [the] village. ” Alaska S tat.
§04.16.220(a)(3) (1980).
Rural villages responded immediately. They held
elections and adopted the alcohol prohibitions authorized by the law. See Report to the Alaska Legislature,
Joint Special Committee on Local Option Laws 2 4
(Mar. 1986)  (“1986 Report”). Many residents, however, soon “ grew frustrated when they found that
their efforts were not succeeding in eradicating alcohol abuse from their communities. ” Berman, supra,
80. “A principal issue of dissatisfaction ” was the “difficulty of enforcing the importation ban with the very
limited local police presence in rural Alaska.” Id.
In 1986, a committee funded by the Alaska legislature submitted a report with shocking findings
about continued alcohol abuse  in rural Alaska.
Throughout the State, villages were being “terrorized
by alcohol abusers.” 1986 Report 1. Nearly every rural
village examined by the com mittee reported significant alcohol-induced problems:
• In Aniak (pop. 475), 95% of the crime was alcohol-related and alcohol was involved in 100%
of the violent crimes.
• In Akiachak (pop. 438), alcohol was the “ number one cause of death for native people.” Many
people had “ committed suicide while intoxicated” and others had “ gotten drunk, disappeared, and ha[d] never been found.”
• In Emmonak (pop. 567), it was “rare that a serious crime, such as sexual assault or homicide, occur[ed] without the involvement of alcohol.” There were “alcohol-related deaths,
drownings and suicides ” and women were

9
“beaten and bec[a]me rape and incest victims
because of alcohol in the home and in the village.”
• In Toksook Bay (pop. 333), the “ biggest problem [was] the number of people  dying alcoholrelated deaths [through] accidents, drownings[,] and murders. ” Families had been
“burned out of their homes in alcohol- related
fires.”
• In Nunapitchuk (pop. 641), “[ a]lcohol-related
drownings [were] a particular problem, ” as
were deaths in alcohol-related fires.
• In Bethel (pop. 4,432), of 150 deaths investigated by troopers, “75 were alcohol-related: 24
were drownings, 11 were suicides, and 15 were
‘very violent, vicious homicides.’”
• In Togiak (pop. 513), “ close to 100% of the police cases [ were] alcohol- related,” including
“suicides in the village” and people being “frozen to death while intoxicated.”
• In Selawik (pop. 545), of the 82 people brought
before the magistrate in 1985, “ all had been
drinking at the time of committing the offense.”
Id. at 32-54. The list went on. See id. 32-61. As one
village public safety officer reported, he had seen “3
good friends die from drownings, … six in plane
crashes, … one person who was murdered, … [and] six
rape victims … all were alcohol related.” Id. at 2. The
sad reality was that “ whenever alcohol is imported
into the village, the whole village goes on an alcohol
binge.” Id. The legislature was urged to use “[ e]very

10
possible tool” available to “ comba[t] the threat posed
by alcohol.” Id. at 109.
Responding to these findings, the Alaska legislature in 1986 empowered local villages to ban the possession of alcohol (and not merely restrict its sale and
importation). Alaska Stat. §04.11.498(a) (1986) .
Among its findings, the legislature concluded that
“the dangers resulting from alcohol abuse are particularly acute in rural areas of the state because the
communities are small, isolated, without adequate
law enforcement, without adequate health care facilities, and populated by people who are closely related
and interdependent.” 1986 Alaska Sess. Laws, ch. 80,
§1(6).
In the decades that followed, there was growing
evidence that the local- option law was working and
that residents in dry villages had “dramatically benefited from reduced alcohol availability. ” M. Landen,
Alcohol-Related Injury Death and Alcohol Availability
in Remote Alaska, 278 JAMA 1755, 1758 (1997) . In
contrast with dry villages, those that allowed alcohol
had “higher rates of both total injury death and alcohol-related injury death among Alaska Natives,” particularly due to “ motor vehicle injury, homicide, and
hypothermia.” Id. at 1757; see also D. Wood, Local Alcohol Prohibition, Police Presence, and Serious Injury
in Isolated Alaska Native Villages, 101 Addiction 393,
394, 398 (2006) (collecting studies).
Even so, alcohol continued to reach villages that
had banned it . Most villages “ lack[ed] a local police
presence to properly enforce local prohibitions,” Wood,
supra, 395, and the State could not fully meet every
local village’s law-enforcement needs, see Alaska Jud.
Council, A Directory of Dispute Resolution in Alaska

11
Outside Federal and State Courts, 8 n.13 (Mar. 1999),
perma.cc/LE8Z-44R7. Alcoholism continued to be an
“endemic condition that ravage [d] individuals, families[,] and communities in rural, particularly Native,
Alaska.” Alaska Commission on Rural Governance
and Empowerment, Final Report to the Governor 12
(June 1999), perma.cc/W87R-AG8J.
The Alaska legislature responded. Legislators introduced legislation to stiffen the penalties by mandating forfeiture of vehicles and airplanes used to
knowingly violate the local- option law. See H.B. 65,
23d Leg., 1st Sess. (Alaska 2003) ; see Letter from
Alaska Ass’n of Chiefs of Police in Support of HB 65
(Apr. 29, 2003), perma.cc/H7US-N9Z8 (noting that villages were “frustrat[ed] with enforcement of the law ”
and urging the legislature to “ creat[e] even more deterrence for someone who is contemplating importation of alcohol into a ‘dry village’”).
The Alaska legislature unanimously adopted
these reforms in 2004. See 2004 Alaska Sess. Laws,
ch. 124, §11; 2004 Alaska House Journal 4175; 2004
Alaska Senate Journal 3647. For vehicles and watercraft used to knowingly transport alcohol into a dry
community, forfeiture became mandatory in specified
circumstances (e.g., for repeat offenders). Alaska Stat.
§04.16.220(i)(2). The court may decline to forfeit a vehicle or watercraft if it is a family ’s sole means of
transportation and, among other things, an innocent
family member depend s on the vessel. Id .
§04.16.220(j). Aircraft were treated more strictly. If a
pilot violates the law by knowingly flying alcohol into
a dry community, forfeiture of the aircraft is mandatory. Id. §04.16.220(i)(1).

12
Today, more than 100 communities in rural
Alaska have voluntarily chosen to restrict the possession or importation of alcohol. Alcoholic Beverages
Control Board, Schedule of Local Option Communities
(Mar. 13, 2024),  perma.cc/YSK3-AQE5. This fact is
widely known . E very pilot should understand  that
“landing with alcohol aboard in villages which prohibit alcohol may result in confiscation of their
aircraft.” Flying in Alaska, Alaska Dep’t of Transp.,
perma.cc/8CFM-UAC6 (emphasis in original). Despite
these bans, villages continue to report that “95 percent of all crimes in rural Alaska can be attributed to
alcohol.” Hearing before the S. Committee on Ind ian
Affairs, 117th Cong. 104 (Dec. 8, 2021) ; see id. at 137
(similar).
C. The Remote Village of Beaver, Alaska
Fourteen miles south of the Arctic Circle, deep in
Alaska’s remote interior, lies the village of Beaver.
The village is home to a mere 48 people. Alaska, 2020
Census Data for Redistricting: Beaver ANVSA ,
perma.cc/XHG9-5YXC. There are no roads in or out of
Beaver. In the winter, temperatures regularly plummet more than 50 degrees below zero. See Beaver
Quick Facts, Tanana Chiefs Confer ence,
perma.cc/EB38-YJC7. If a medical emergency arises,
the nearest hospital is in Fairbanks, over 100 miles of
wilderness away. In Beaver, “[a]ll it takes is one little
mistake” to ruin a life. K. Johnson, On Alaska’s Coldest Days, a Village Draws Close for Warmth , N.Y.
Times (Jan. 31, 2017).
Before 2004, Beaver allowed alcohol in the village,
but attitudes changed as alcohol arrived “bottle by
bottle, via airplane, snowmachine, and boat. ” J. Gay,
Death Spurs Village to Ban Booze, Anchorage Daily

13
News (Aug. 15, 2004). On December 10, 2003, 21-yearold Arvin Petruska, a resident of Beaver, died after a
night of drinking, having passed out outdoors where
the temperature had fallen to 18 below zero.
Petruska’s death was a turning point, galvanizing the
village to call for a referendum to prohibit alcohol and
its importation into the community. The referendum
passed the following year by a vote of 17-11. Following
the election, the village “told the airlines that fly into
Beaver not to haul anyone who is carrying booze.” Id.
At the time, the village recognized that it was “ going
to be hard” to enforce the law and that the new rules
would not work if “ individuals within the village …
continue to bring in alcohol.” Id.
D. Procedural History
On April 3, 2012,  Kenneth Jouppi arrived at the
Fairbanks Airport to fly a passenger to Beaver .
App.32a. Also at the airport were Alaska state troopers, who had a warrant to search Jouppi’s plane. The
State had been investigating Jouppi and his company,
Ken Air, LLC, after receiving information that Jouppi
had repeatedly transported passengers with alcohol to
local-option communities . Tr.18:17-19:4; 29:4- 30:4
(Oct. 17, 2013) ; State v. Jouppi , 397 P.3d 1026, 1028
(Alaska Ct. App. 2017).1
Troopers watched Jouppi load his plane with various boxes and bags. Tr.18:12-19:5 (Aug. 20, 2013). As
Jouppi started the engine and prepared to take off, the

SUMMARY OF THE ARGUMENT
The Eighth Amendment prohibits “ excessive
fines.” An excessive fine “surpass[es] the usual , the
proper, or a normal measure of proportion. ” Bajakajian, 524 U.S. at 335. Since the Founding, Congress has ordered the  forfeiture of vessels us ed in
crimes, including customs fraud, the slave trade, piracy, and more. These laws were critical to stripping
offenders of the means to repeat crimes and deterring
future violations.
In the modern era, civil forfeiture has grown in
ways that many find troubling. But not all forfeiture
is the same. Criminal forfeiture (like here) occurs only
after a defendant has been found guilty of a crime. It

17
thus provides the due -process protections  that civil
forfeiture might not.
State legislatures are tasked with determining
punishments for convicted defendants, and their determinations must receive “‘substantial deference. ’”
Id. at 336. When a convicted defendant fits within the
class of persons targeted by the law and he caused the
same potential for harm feared by the legislature, it is
not a court’s role to second-guess the legislature’s determination that forfeiture of the instrumentality of
his offense is warranted. Courts that respect these decisions are not assessing the gravity of an offense
“purely in the abstract.” Pet-Br.13. They are refusing
to override reasoned determinations by the people’ s
representatives about how best to stop crime.
Here, the forfeiture of Jouppi’s plane was not “excessive.” For more than a half century, Alaska has
been combatting the scourge of alcohol abuse in its rural communities. To protect its villages, Alaska followed a formula as old as  the Founding: mandat ory
forfeiture of a vessel used to knowingly commit a
crime. Alaska’s law prevents convicted offenders from
using an airplane to once again fly alcohol into a dry
village and deters others from doing the same.
Jouppi insists that the Alaska Supreme Court refused to consider Jouppi’ s “own wrongdoing. ” Pet-
Br.32. Not so. The court reviewed and considered all
the facts that led up to Jouppi ’s conviction for knowingly transporting alcohol into a dry village. Jouppi’ s
actions fell squarely within the c onduct targeted by
the law, and he threatened to cause the same harm
feared by the legislature. Whether Jouppi knew about
all or just some of the nine gallons of beer he loaded

18
onto his plane does not change the constitutional analysis.
Those most affected by Jouppi’s crime do not find
this forfeiture excessive. The Alaska legislature unanimously agreed that the best way to enforce local bans
was by mandating the forfeiture of the airplane used
to knowingly bring alcohol into the community. And
the residents of the remote village of Beaver voted to
ban the importation of alcohol into their community.
These were reasonable decisions that fall squarely
within the powers of the people’s representatives and
the people themselves. The judgment below should be
affirmed.
ARGUMENT
I. Legislatures may require convicted
defendants to forfeit the undisputed
instrumentality of a crime without
violating the Excessive Fines Clause.
The Eighth Amendment provides: “Excessive bail
shall not be required, nor excessive fines imposed, nor
cruel and unusual punishments inflicted. ” This case
presents the question of whether the criminal forfeiture of an airplane used by a convicted defendant to
knowingly transport alcohol into a dry village in
Alaska violates the Excessive Fines Clause. The text,
history, and this Court ’s precedent provide the answer. A legislature can protect its citizens through the
mandatory forfeiture of the instruments  of crimes
without running afoul of the Excessive Fines Clause.
A. The forfeiture of vessels used to commit
crimes has a long history and tradition.
1. Since the Founding, Congress has authorized
the f orfeiture of vessels used to commit  crimes. In

19

States only to return  with the goods to a different

ch. 5, §34, 1 Stat. 29, 46. The law mandated that  “all
persons concerned therein, shall, on indictment and
conviction thereof, suffer imprisonment for a term not
exceeding six months. ” Id. The law also imposed forfeiture of the ship used in the crime: “[A]ll such goods,
wares and merchandise shall be subject to seizure and

goods shall be landed, and the vessels or boats used in

A few years later, Congress enacted the Neutrality Act of 1794 to keep private citizens from entangling the United States in foreign wars . See Act of
June 5, 1794, ch. 50, 1 Stat. 381. Congress made it unlawful to, among other things, fit out “any ship or vessel with intent that such ship or vessel shall be employed in the service of any foreign prince or state” to

United States are at peace. ” Id. §3, 1 Stat. at 383.
Those found in violation of the law faced up to $5,000

ordering that “every such ship or vessel with her
tackle, apparel and furniture together … shall be forfeited.” Id.; see also Act of April 20, 1818, ch. 88, §3, 3
Stat. 447, 448 (similar).
Congress similarly employed forfeitures to prevent the importation of enslaved persons. In 1800,
Congress made it “unlawful for any citizen of the
United States or other person residing therein, to

70, 70. When any such ship was captured, Congress

When Congress later  enacted a complete ban on

21

“removing from circulation the ‘ instrumentalities’ of

B. The demanding burden of proof in
criminal forfeiture proceedings protects
innocent property owners from wrongful
forfeiture.
An Excessive Fines Clause analysis requires an

524 U.S. at 339, and legislatures can ensure that the
toughest penalties are applied to the most culpable offenders. One way is through the offender ’s mens rea.
“Most would agree that negligent conduct is less serious than intentional conduct. ” Solem v. Helm , 463
U.S. 277, 293 (1983). “Historically,” criminal law was
“based upon a theory of punishing the vicious will. ”
Morissette v. United States, 342 U.S. 246, 250 n.4

the offender was “a free agent confronted with a choice
between doing right and doing wrong and choosing
freely to do wrong.” Id.
In the forfeiture context, an offender ’s decision to
act knowingly and intentional ly has long confirmed
the appropriateness of a forfeiture. Most notably, the

“vessel or boat with its tackle” that were used to violate the law “shall be forfeited.” Act of March 3, 1791,

Alexander Hamilton 82-83 (1966) (emphasis added).

mens rea is a hallmark of in personam criminal forfeiture, the procedure that Alaska followed here. For

C. A legislature’s determination of the
gravity of a criminal offense is entitled
to substantial deference.
1. In Bajakajian , the Court stressed that “ judgments about the appropriate punishment for an offense belong in the first instance to the legislature. ”
524 U.S. at 336. The fixing of a punishment for a crime
“involves a substantive penological judgment that, as
a general matter, is ‘properly within the province of
legislatures, not courts. ’” Harmelin v. Michigan, 501
U.S. 957, 998 (1991) (Kennedy, J., concurring in part)
(quoting Rummel v. Estelle , 445 U.S. 263, 275- 76
(1980)). Any determinations about the “ nature and
purposes of punishment for criminal acts implicate
difficult and enduring questions respecting the sanctity of the individual, the nature of law, and the relation between law and the social order. ” Id. The “responsibility for making these fundamental choices
and implementing them lies with the legislature.” Id.;
see Gore v. United States, 357 U.S. 386, 393 (1958)
(“Whatever views may be entertained regarding severity of punishment, whether one believes in its efficacy or its futility, … these are peculiarly questions of
legislative policy.”).
Given the legislature’ s primacy in this field, this
Court has a “longstanding” “tradition of deferring to
state legislatures in making and implementing” these
types of “ policy decisions. ” Ewing v. California , 538
U.S. 11, 24 (2003)  (plurality op inion). Courts thus
must grant “ substantial deference to the broad authority that legislatures necessarily possess in determining the types and limits of punishments for

31
crimes.” Harmelin, 501 U.S. at 999 (Kennedy, J., concurring in part) . The same “ ‘substantial deference ’”
applies in Excessive Fines cases such as this one. Bajakajian, 524 U.S. at 336.
To be sure, “ ‘substantial deference, ’” id., is not
blind deference. The Excessive Fines Clause stands as
a bulwark against government overreach, and legislatures are not immune from its oversight. See, e.g. ,
Timbs, 586 U.S. at  153 (discussing the Black Codes
used to “subjugate newly freed slaves”). But when the
legislature makes a reasonable judgment about the
gravity of a knowing criminal offense, that determination should not be lightly disturbed.
In practice, this deference means a forfeiture
should fail the “ gross disproportionality principle ”
“only in the ‘ exceedingly rare’ and ‘extreme’ case.”
Lockyer v. Andrade, 538 U.S. 63, 73 (2003) (quoting
Harmelin, 501 U.S. at 1001 (Kennedy, J., concurring

gravity of an offense warrants forfeiture of the instrumentality of the offense. Pet-Br.34-36. The Court has
long recognized that “Eighth Amendment judgments

would “invite a grand ‘ balancing test in which unweighted factors mysteriously are weighed. ’” June

multi-factor “framework is so unpredictable that it
fails to provide meaningful protection [,]” because the
outcome will “depen[d] heavily on which factors the
judge considers and how much weight he accords each
of them. ” Crawford v. Washington , 541 U.S. 36, 63
(2004).

defendant “fit into the class of persons for whom the
statute was principally designed. ” 524 U.S. at 338.
That focus respected the legislative deference that undergirds the gross disp roportionality standard. Once
the legislature makes a judgment to outlaw certain
conduct, that judgment by the people ’s representatives gets deference. The question that remains for
courts is whether the defendant falls within the class
of persons for whom  the statute was principally designed. If he does, the defendant faces a heavy burden
proving that the forfeiture is unconstitutional. Harmelin, 501 U.S. at 998-99 (Kennedy, J., concurring in
part); Rummel, 445 U.S. at 274-76.

caused by the defendant as part of the gross disproportionality analysis. Bajakajian’s crime was “solely a

35

a relatively minor way.” 524 U.S. at 337, 339. “Had his
crime gone undetected, the Government would have

had left the country. ” Id. The Court thus found the
harm caused by his reporting offense to be “minimal.”
524 U.S. at 339.
Pointing to Bajakajian, Jouppi appears to believe
that the gravity of an offense is low unless actual
harm (a death, a violent act, and the like) materializes. Pet-Br.39. But since the Founding, Congress has
ordered the forfeiture of vessels used to commit crimes
regardless of whether the harms were actually realized. E.g., Act of June 5, 1794, ch. 50, §3, 1 Stat. at 383
(requiring forfeiture when there was an “ intent that
such ship or vessel ” be used to commit hostilities
against another nation). As the history shows, often
“the evil to be corrected relates to apparent danger,
rather than to actual injury sustained. ” J. Bishop,
Commentaries on the Criminal Law, §682 (1868); e.g.,
Minor v. State, 605 A.2d 138, 141 (Md. 1992) (“It is the
reckless conduct and not the harm caused by the conduct, if any, which the statute was intended to criminalize.”). There is “no doubt that preventing danger to
the community is a legitimate regulatory goal. ”
United States v. Salerno, 481 U.S. 739, 747 (1987).
When assessing the gravity of the harm, then, a
court is not limited to only actual harm the defendant
perpetrated before he was caught. The court must also
consider the “harm caused or threatened to the victim
or society.” Solem, 463 U.S. at 292 (emphasis added);
see TXO Prod. Corp. v. All. Res. Corp., 509 U.S. 443,
460 (1993)  (plurality opinion) (court must “ consider

the magnitude of the potential harm that the defendant’s conduct” could have caused if “the wrongful plan
had succeeded,” as well as the “possible harm to other
victims that might have resulted if similar future behavior were not deterred”).

driving. Many States authorize the forfeiture of cars

drunk driving. See, e.g. , Ariz. Rev. Stat. §28 -1384(A)

the motor vehicle owned and operated by the person
at the time of the offense forfeited.”). The forfeiture of
the car in these circumstances has the obvious benefit

drive on a regular basis to commit those offenses in

(Ohio 2022).
But whether the driver actually kills someone or
only risks killing someone does not change the constitutional analysis. Because the drunk driver “ plays
Russian roulette every time he or she drives on the
road,” id. at 684, a legislature could reasonably determine that any drunk driving is dangerous enough to
warrant forfeiture of the car. See County of Nassau v.
Canavan, 802 N.E.2d 616, 622 (N.Y. 2003) (“Given the
gravity of the crime of drunk driving, it is difficult to
imagine that forfeiture of an automobile for such a
crime could ever be excessive.”). Nothing in the Constitution precludes legislatures from designing penological schemes to stop dangerous activity before it
kills by requiring forfeiture of the undisputed instrumentality of a crime.

Pet-Br.9, 16, because Bajakajian was not in the class
of people targeted by the law. His crime was just a “reporting offense” and his actions were never going to
injure anyone. 524 U.S. at 337. If Bajakajian had been
a “money launderer, a drug trafficker, or a tax
evader,” id. at 338, then of course this Court would
have considered the harms from laundering money,
trafficking in drugs, and evading taxes. So too here.
Jouppi was within the class of persons principally targeted by the statute and, unlike Bajakajian, knowingly threatened t he exact harm the Alaska legislature sought to prevent.
More fundamentally, what Jouppi seeks is a world
in which courts routinely engage in case- by-case,

49
second-guessing of a legislature’ s scheme to determine whether forfeiture of an instrument of a crime is
really warranted. Pet-Br.19. To Jouppi, it can never
be enough that a defendant is convicted of a knowing
criminal offense; that he fits within the class of pilots
that the law was designed to stop; that he threatened
to cause the same harm targeted by the legislature;
and that the airplane was the instrumentality of the
crime. Instead, Jouppi would have courts weigh an indefinite number of factors each time to determine the
appropriate punishment.
Here, the people of Beaver, in the wake of the
death of one of its young residents, voted to b an alcohol in their village. And the Alaska legislature, after
a decades -long fight combatting alcohol- related violence, crime, and death in rural Alaska, unanimously
adopted a reasonable scheme of deterrence and incapacitation to address the crisis. When assessing that
decision, it is “enough that the State of [Alaska] has a
reasonable basis for believing that” the punishment it
selected—the forfeiture of airplanes convicted defendants have used to knowingly transport alcohol into dry
villages—“advances the goals of its criminal justice
system in any substantial way.” Ewing, 538 U.S. at 28
(plurality opinion) (cleaned up).  Nothing in Jouppi ’s
particular circumstances warrants overturning the
determinations of the Alaska legislature and the residents of Beaver.
CONCLUSION
 The judgment should be affirmed.
